blurb: Metals, plastics, elastomers, ceramics, glass, composites, and functional materials — compared on strength-to-weight, service temperature, cost per kg, and how you shape them.
question: What should this part be made of?
title: Engineering Materials: A Practical Reference
lede: Material choice sets a part's weight, cost, and service life before anyone picks a process. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} engineering materials across seven classes, from mild steel at about $1/kg to infrared crystals at a thousand times that, with the property, processing, and supply context that decides what you can actually specify.

parts.name: Ferrous Alloys
parts.blurb: steel and iron, the default structural metals

parts.name: Nonferrous Alloys
parts.blurb: aluminum, titanium, copper, and the hot metals

parts.name: Ceramics, Glass & Carbon
parts.blurb: hard, brittle, and stable at high temperature

parts.name: Composites
parts.blurb: fiber plus matrix, with properties per direction

parts.name: Functional Materials
parts.blurb: specified for magnetics, heat flow, or light

groupBlurbs.Carbon and alloy steel: the default structural metal, at about $1/kg
groupBlurbs.Stainless steel: corrosion resistance for four times the steel price
groupBlurbs.Cast iron: cheap complex castings that damp vibration
groupBlurbs.Light alloys: aluminum, magnesium, and titanium for weight
groupBlurbs.Copper and high-temperature alloys: conduct electricity or survive the hot section
groupBlurbs.Commodity plastics: the cheap plastics, under $2 per kilogram
groupBlurbs.Engineering plastics: molded parts that carry real mechanical load
groupBlurbs.Thermoset resins: cured once, so they cannot be remelted
groupBlurbs.Elastomers: rubber that seals, damps, and springs back
groupBlurbs.Polymer composites: fiber carries the load, resin holds it in place
groupBlurbs.Metal and ceramic composites: reinforcement in a matrix that tolerates heat
groupBlurbs.Magnetic materials: chosen for the shape of their B-H curve
groupBlurbs.Thermal and optical materials: move heat or pass light on spec

facets.label: Picked for
facets.tip: What engineers usually specify the family for. Directional, not exhaustive: most materials do several of these adequately, so the tags mark the reasons someone reaches for this family first. Corrosion covers chemical resistance too, and Sealing covers damping and cushioning.

facets.label: Strength/wt
facets.tip: Specific strength: tensile strength (flexural for ceramics) divided by density, in kN·m/kg, which is the same number as MPa per g/cm³. Mild steel is about 50, 6061-T6 aluminum 115, Ti-6Al-4V 215, and a quasi-isotropic carbon laminate 350–400. Figures are for a common structural grade of the family. Untagged where the material is not chosen to carry load.

facets.label: Max temp
facets.tip: Maximum continuous service temperature in air for a common grade, in °C, not a brief excursion. Polymers are limited by softening and oxidation, metals by creep and scaling, ceramics mostly by what they react with. Graphite and refractory metals only reach the top band in vacuum or inert gas.

facets.label: Processing
facets.tip: How parts are usually made from the material, which is often the binding constraint. Forming covers rolling, extrusion, forging, stamping, and hot glass work · Casting covers die, investment, and sand · Sintering covers powder metallurgy and ceramic firing · Layup covers hand layup, prepreg, and filament winding. The processes themselves are on the manufacturing-processes sheet.

facets.label: Cost/kg
facets.tip: Directional price per kilogram of the usual mill or feedstock form in commercial quantity, not the finished part. Bands: <$2 · $2–10 · $10–50 · $50–200 · $200+. Machining, scrap rate, and qualification usually cost more than the material, so treat this as a floor rather than a budget.
